claim: HIV-1 capsid comprises 1000–1500 copies of a single viral protein, CA.
source: The HIV capsid comprises 1000–1500 copies of a single viral protein, CA, corresponding to less than half of the total CA released by proteolytic processing of the Gag polyprotein during maturation (Briggs et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Briggs et al., 2004

claim: CA incorporated into the capsid corresponds to less than half of the total CA released by proteolytic processing of the Gag polyprotein during maturation.
source: The HIV capsid comprises 1000–1500 copies of a single viral protein, CA, corresponding to less than half of the total CA released by proteolytic processing of the Gag polyprotein during maturation (Briggs et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Briggs et al., 2004

claim: CA is a two-domain protein which can form both hexameric and pentameric assemblies.
source: CA is a two-domain protein, which can form both hexameric and pentameric assemblies.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about CA protein structure

claim: The conical capsid is a fullerene structure which incorporates 12 pentamers into the otherwise hexameric lattice.
source: The conical capsid is a fullerene structure, which incorporates 12 pentamers into the otherwise hexameric lattice, a geometric constraint that must be satisfied in order to achieve capsid closure (Li et al., 2000; Pornillos et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2000 and Pornillos et al., 2011

claim: Incorporation of 12 pentamers is a geometric constraint that must be satisfied in order to achieve capsid closure.
source: The conical capsid is a fullerene structure, which incorporates 12 pentamers into the otherwise hexameric lattice, a geometric constraint that must be satisfied in order to achieve capsid closure (Li et al., 2000; Pornillos et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2000 and Pornillos et al., 2011

claim: HIV capsids have an average length of 119 nm and an average width of 61 nm.
source: Typically, capsids have a conical shape with an average length of 119 nm and an average width of 61 nm (Briggs et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Briggs et al., 2003

claim: A large fraction of viral particles contain 'defective' capsids which do not have closed surfaces.
source: In addition, a large fraction of viral particles contain 'defective' capsids, which do not have closed surfaces (Frank et al., 2015; Mattei et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frank et al., 2015; Mattei et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2013

claim: GFP-positive particles released from HEK293T cells decreased by 99.7% when viral release was blocked.
source: The number of GFP-positive particles in the cell supernatant decreased by 99.7% when viral release was blocked (Figure 1B), confirming that essentially all GFP-positive particles released in the absence of the block represent viral particles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Essentially all GFP-positive particles released in the absence of the block represent viral particles.
source: The number of GFP-positive particles in the cell supernatant decreased by 99.7% when viral release was blocked (Figure 1B), confirming that essentially all GFP-positive particles released in the absence of the block represent viral particles.
evidence: Inferred from the 99.7% decrease when release is blocked

claim: PFO efficiently permeabilized the viral membrane by assembling into characteristic ring-shaped membrane pores with a mean pore diameter of about 35 nm.
source: PFO efficiently permeabilized the viral membrane by assembling into characteristic ring-shaped membrane pores with a mean pore diameter of about 35 nm (Figure 1D and E), consistent with its activity on cholesterol-containing membranes (Dang et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and E and citation to Dang et al., 2005

claim: PFO pores are sufficiently large to permit the passage of proteins while the viral core is retained within the perforated viral membrane.
source: These pores are sufficiently large to permit the passage of proteins while the viral core is retained within the perforated viral membrane allowing the core to be observed over time while it can undergo disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the pore size of ~35 nm and the ability to observe cores over time

claim: The mean fraction of encapsidated GFP is approximately 13%.
source: This fraction was consistent with the amount of GFP expected to be randomly trapped inside the volume of the capsid (relative to the volume of the viral particle) during maturation.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The fraction of encapsidated GFP is consistent with the ratio of the volume inside the capsid to the total volume of the viral particle (16%).
source: The mean fraction of encapsidated GFP is ~13%, similar to the ratio of the volume inside the capsid to the total volume of the viral particle (16%), which was estimated on the basis of the following considerations.
evidence: Supported by calculation and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Leaky capsids constituted the largest fraction of particles (60–80%), irrespective of which type of capsid-binding molecules were present in the solution.
source: Leaky capsids constituted the largest fraction of particles (60–80%), irrespective of which type of capsid-binding molecules were present in the solution.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The half-life of capsid opening in the absence of capsid-binding molecules is 8 minutes.
source: The survival curve of intact capsids (i.e. those that remain positive for encapsidated GFP) exposed to buffer without additives could be approximated with an exponential decay function (Figure 2B, black lines and Figure 2—source data 1) yielding an estimate for the capsid half-life of 8 min (Figure 2C), which is similar to a previous estimate of 10 min for the half-life of capsid uncoating in vitro (Francis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and 2C, and citation to Francis et al., 2016

claim: A sub-population of capsids (~20%) opened with a half-life of less than 1 minute.
source: Fitting a bi-exponential decay made it possible to quantify a sub-population of capsids (~20%) that were substantially less stable and opened with a half-life of less than 1 min (Figure 2B, dashed grey line and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by bi-exponential fitting of data in Figure 2B

claim: The E45A mutation in CA yields hyperstable capsids.
source: To validate that the GFP release kinetics depend on capsid stability, we assessed the effect of the E45A mutation in CA on capsid opening. This mutation is known to yield hyperstable capsids (Forshey et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2012), which was also apparent in our capsid opening assay with a 4.5-fold increase in half-life compared to capsids assembled from wild-type CA (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Forshey et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2012 and experimental data in Figure 2C

claim: CA E45A mutation results in a 4.5-fold increase in capsid opening half-life compared to wild-type CA.
source: This mutation is known to yield hyperstable capsids (Forshey et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2012), which was also apparent in our capsid opening assay with a 4.5-fold increase in half-life compared to capsids assembled from wild-type CA (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2C

claim: CypA at 1 μM had no effect on capsid half-life.
source: In our assay, CypA had no effect on capsid half-life when added at a concentration of 1 μM and lead to an approximately two-fold increase in half-life at 20 μM (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2C

claim: CypA at 20 μM leads to an approximately two-fold increase in capsid half-life.
source: In our assay, CypA had no effect on capsid half-life when added at a concentration of 1 μM and lead to an approximately two-fold increase in half-life at 20 μM (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2C

claim: PF74 accelerates capsid opening with a half-life of 41 seconds.
source: Addition of these inhibitors to the capsid opening assay at high concentrations within the range typically used in cellular and biochemical assays revealed an increase in the ratio of opening to closed particles after 30 min (Figure 2A) and a pronounced acceleration of capsid opening with half-lives of 41 s and 2.4 min, respectively (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2A and 2C

claim: BI2 accelerates capsid opening with a half-life of 2.4 minutes.
source: Addition of these inhibitors to the capsid opening assay at high concentrations within the range typically used in cellular and biochemical assays revealed an increase in the ratio of opening to closed particles after 30 min (Figure 2A) and a pronounced acceleration of capsid opening with half-lives of 41 s and 2.4 min, respectively (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2A and 2C

claim: Hexacarboxybenzene strongly inhibits capsid opening.
source: In contrast, the small molecule hexacarboxybenzene (C6(COOH)6), which binds to hexameric CA (Jacques et al., 2016), showed the opposite effect by strongly inhibiting capsid opening (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2A and citation to Jacques et al., 2016

claim: The half-lives of capsids in the presence of 10 and 1000 μM hexacarboxybenzene were estimated to be in the order of 1 hr and 10 hr, respectively.
source: There was an insufficient number of opening events to allow a robust fit of the survival curves but we estimated that the half-lives in the presence of 10 and 1000 μM hexacarboxybenzene were in the order of 1 hr and 10 hr, respectively.
evidence: Estimated from limited data due to insufficient opening events

claim: CypA binding to the capsid is completely abolished in the presence of cyclosporin A.
source: However, binding of CypA was completely abolished in the presence of the competitive inhibitor cyclosporin A, which binds to the binding pocket on CypA (Figure 3C, bottom panels) (Mikol et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3C and citation to Mikol et al., 1993

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for the CypA-capsid interaction is 10–12 μM.
source: Analysis of the equilibrium binding levels gave an estimate of the KD of 10–12 μM with an estimated 500–1000 molecules bound per capsid at saturation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: An estimated 500–1000 CypA molecules are bound per capsid at saturation.
source: Analysis of the equilibrium binding levels gave an estimate of the KD of 10–12 μM with an estimated 500–1000 molecules bound per capsid at saturation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The number of CypA binding sites represents roughly half of the number of CA proteins in an assembled capsid.
source: This number of sites represents roughly half of the number of CA proteins in an assembled capsid (Briggs et al., 2003).
evidence: Inferred from the estimated 500-1000 binding sites and citation to Briggs et al., 2003

claim: The expected CypA:CA ratio at saturation is 1:2.
source: The expected CypA:CA ratio at saturation is also 1:2, because binding to both cyclophilin loops of CA molecules connecting neighboring hexamers in the lattice would lead to steric clashes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016 and inference about steric clashes

claim: The lattice is completely coated with CypA at saturation.
source: This observation suggests that the lattice is completely coated with CypA at saturation, and that binding sites on different locations of the capsid are equivalent.
evidence: Inferred from the 1:2 CypA:CA ratio and the number of binding sites

claim: Binding sites on different locations of the capsid are equivalent.
source: This observation suggests that the lattice is completely coated with CypA at saturation, and that binding sites on different locations of the capsid are equivalent.
evidence: Inferred from the binding data showing uniform saturation

claim: The majority of CypA fluorescence signal (85%) disappeared rapidly with a rate of 1.5 s−1 after removal from solution.
source: The majority of the fluorescence signal (85%) disappeared rapidly with a rate of 1.5 s−1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3F

claim: The off-rate of CypA measured may be limited by mass transport.
source: This rate was close to the rate of solution exchange achievable in our microfluidic set-up, such that the off-rate of CypA measured here may be limited by mass transport.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of measured rate to solution exchange rate

claim: SPR measurements gave a KD of 21.8 μM for CypA interaction with immobilized CA.
source: Equilibrium binding analysis of the SPR data gave a KD of 21.8 μM and 19 μM for interaction with immobilized CA (consistent with previous data [Yoo et al., 1997]) and CA hexamer (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), respectively
evidence: Supported by SPR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and citation to Yoo et al., 1997

claim: SPR measurements gave a KD of 19 μM for CypA interaction with CA hexamer.
source: Equilibrium binding analysis of the SPR data gave a KD of 21.8 μM and 19 μM for interaction with immobilized CA (consistent with previous data [Yoo et al., 1997]) and CA hexamer (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), respectively
evidence: Supported by SPR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The off-rates for CypA from CA and CA hexamer determined by SPR were 4 ± 0.3 s−1 and 3.5 ± 0.4 s−1, respectively.
source: while the off-rates determined after removal of CypA from solution were 4 ± 0.3 s−1 and 3.5 ± 0.4 s−1, respectively.
evidence: Supported by SPR measurements

claim: CypA binding does not have a measurable effect on capsid opening when used at concentrations of up to 1 μM.
source: Firstly, CypA binding does not have a measurable effect on capsid opening when used at concentrations of up to 1 μM (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2C

claim: CypA binds (and dissociates) with fast rates to binding sites all over the surface of the lattice.
source: Secondly, CypA binds (and dissociates) with fast rates to binding sites all over the surface of the lattice (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3

claim: Particles with leaky capsids contain a CA lattice that is poised to fall apart and only persists for a short period of time before disassembly.
source: We interpreted this signal as follows: particles with leaky capsids contain a CA lattice that is poised to fall apart and only persists for a short period of time before disassembly.
evidence: Interpretation of CypA paint data for leaky capsids

claim: The median disassembly kinetics after capsid opening were governed by a half-life of approximately 70–100 s.
source: The median disassembly kinetics after capsid opening (Figure 4E, right heatmap) were governed by a half-life of approximately 70–100 s.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4E

claim: Capsid opening is the rate-limiting step for capsid uncoating.
source: We conclude that capsid opening is the rate-limiting step for capsid uncoating, and lattice disassembly will proceed rapidly once the capsid has developed the first defect.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that disassembly proceeds rapidly after opening

claim: Lattice disassembly will proceed rapidly once the capsid has developed the first defect.
source: We conclude that capsid opening is the rate-limiting step for capsid uncoating, and lattice disassembly will proceed rapidly once the capsid has developed the first defect.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid disassembly kinetics observed after opening

claim: In the presence of PF74, no decrease in the CypA paint signal was observed after capsid opening.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of PF74, we observed no decrease in the CypA paint signal after capsid opening (Figure 5B, right heatmap).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5B

claim: PF74 stabilizes the lattice such that no (further) CA proteins are released from the lattice after opening.
source: This observation suggests that the lattice develops a defect to allow the passage of proteins but is otherwise highly stabilized such that no (further) CA proteins are released from the lattice.
evidence: Inferred from the constant CypA paint signal after opening in the presence of PF74

claim: The amount of CA protein lost during the opening step in the presence of PF74 was below the limit of detection.
source: The amount of CA protein lost during the opening step was below the limit of detection in our assay (compare the CypA paint intensity histograms before and after capsid opening, Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5B

claim: Hexacarboxybenzene only had a modest stabilizing effect on the CA lattice after capsid opening.
source: In contrast to the strong stabilization observed with PF74, hexacarboxybenzene only had a modest stabilizing effect on the CA lattice after capsid opening, as seen from the CypA paint signal decay from that point onwards (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5D

claim: PF74 promotes a structural change leading to a defect in the capsid that allows passage of proteins.
source: We conclude that while PF74 promotes a structural change leading to a defect in the capsid that allows passage of proteins, only little (if any) CA protein is lost during this step, and the remaining lattice is highly stabilized.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PF74 accelerates opening but stabilizes the remaining lattice

claim: Only little (if any) CA protein is lost during the PF74-induced opening step.
source: We conclude that while PF74 promotes a structural change leading to a defect in the capsid that allows passage of proteins, only little (if any) CA protein is lost during this step, and the remaining lattice is highly stabilized.
evidence: Inferred from the CypA paint data showing no decrease in signal

claim: The remaining lattice is highly stabilized after PF74-induced opening.
source: We conclude that while PF74 promotes a structural change leading to a defect in the capsid that allows passage of proteins, only little (if any) CA protein is lost during this step, and the remaining lattice is highly stabilized.
evidence: Inferred from the constant CypA paint signal after opening

claim: Hexacarboxybenzene strongly inhibits capsid opening but has little effect on uncoating once the process has started.
source: In contrast, hexacarboxybenzene strongly inhibits capsid opening but has little effect on uncoating once the process has started.
evidence: Inferred from the delayed opening but continued disassembly in the presence of hexacarboxybenzene

claim: Cell lysate slows capsid opening with a four-fold increase in the half-life of this process.
source: However, capsid opening was slowed down with a four-fold increase in the half-life of this process (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6A and B

claim: The number of CypA molecules bound on intact (closed) capsids at equilibrium in the presence of cell lysate was comparable to that measured in buffer.

evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: There was no competition with endogenous CypA in cell lysate due to the high dilution factor used.
source: The number of CypA molecules bound on intact (closed) capsids at equilibrium was comparable to that measured in buffer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that there was no competition with endogenous CypA due to the high dilution factor used in this experiment.
evidence: Inferred from the comparable binding levels in buffer and lysate

claim: The process of uncoating in diluted cell lysate is in principle the same as in buffer, with the lattice falling apart shortly after it had opened up, albeit with a slightly reduced rate.
source: CypA paint revealed that the process of uncoating in diluted cell lysate was in principle the same as is buffer, with the lattice falling apart shortly after it had opened up, albeit with a slightly reduced rate (Figure 6D and E).

claim: The stabilizing effect exerted by the diluted cell lysate is consistent with previous observations.
source: The stabilizing effect exerted by the diluted cell lysate is consistent with previous observations (Francis et al., 2016; Fricke et al., 2013; Guth and Sodroski, 2014), and it may be amplified when components are present at cytosolic concentrations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Francis et al., 2016; Fricke et al., 2013; Guth and Sodroski, 2014

claim: The stabilizing effect of cell lysate may be amplified when components are present at cytosolic concentrations.
source: The stabilizing effect exerted by the diluted cell lysate is consistent with previous observations (Francis et al., 2016; Fricke et al., 2013; Guth and Sodroski, 2014), and it may be amplified when components are present at cytosolic concentrations.
evidence: Speculation about the effect at higher concentrations

claim: Opening of the first defect in the lattice is the rate-limiting step of uncoating.
source: Opening of the first defect in the lattice is the rate-limiting step of uncoating, which is followed by rapid, catastrophic collapse.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of rapid disassembly after opening

claim: Capsid opening is followed by rapid, catastrophic collapse.
source: Opening of the first defect in the lattice is the rate-limiting step of uncoating, which is followed by rapid, catastrophic collapse.

claim: The capsid-binding inhibitor PF74 accelerates capsid opening but stabilizes the remaining lattice.
source: The capsid-binding inhibitor PF74 accelerates capsid opening but stabilizes the remaining lattice.

claim: Binding of a polyanion to a conserved arginine cluster in the lattice strongly delays initiation of uncoating but does not prevent subsequent lattice disassembly.

claim: Different stages of uncoating can be controlled independently.
source: Our observations suggest that different stages of uncoating can be controlled independently with the interplay between different capsid-binding regulators likely to determine the overall uncoating kinetics.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of PF74 and hexacarboxybenzene on opening vs. disassembly

claim: The interplay between different capsid-binding regulators is likely to determine the overall uncoating kinetics.
source: Our observations suggest that different stages of uncoating can be controlled independently with the interplay between different capsid-binding regulators likely to determine the overall uncoating kinetics.

source: We now know that the capsid plays a key role in these processes and is critical for successful infection.

claim: The capsid must disassemble to release the viral DNA at the appropriate place and time.

claim: The defect could rapidly propagate via dissociation of CA subunits that are no longer stabilized by dimer and/or trimer interfaces linking neighboring hexamers in the lattice.

claim: The interactions between subunits in a hexamer (or pentamer) represent a weak link in the CA lattice.

claim: Hexacarboxybenzene stabilizes the hexamer by binding in its central electropositive pore.

claim: Hexacarboxybenzene leads to an increase in the energy barrier for dissociation of the first CA molecule(s), but only if the surrounding lattice is intact.

claim: In the absence of capsid binders, uncoating is an all-or-none process that proceeds rapidly after the first defect is created.
source: (2) In the absence of capsid binders, uncoating is an all-or-none process that proceeds rapidly after the first defect is created.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of rapid disassembly after opening

claim: Capsid-binding molecules exhibit differential effects on the steps that control initiation and continuation of uncoating.
source: (3) Capsid-binding molecules exhibit differential effects on the steps that control initiation and continuation of uncoating.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations with PF74 and hexacarboxybenzene
